  "content": "STATUTORY ARCHITECTURE: ID ACT, IR CODE, STANDING ORDERS, S&E ACTS
Reference handout — Employee Relations Management: Indian Statutory Framework & Practice

HOW TO USE THIS HANDOUT
Indian employee relations law is not one statute. For any given workplace, at least three or four layers can apply simultaneously: a central industrial relations statute, a central standing-orders statute (or its successor), and a state-specific shops and establishments statute. None of these substitute for the others. A practitioner's first task for any establishment is to work out which layers actually apply — that is the point of this handout. Every threshold cited below is a statutory figure and is subject to amendment by Parliament, by state legislatures (labour is a Concurrent List subject — Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List III, Entries 22 and 24), and by state-specific amendments to central Acts. Always verify the current, state-applicable figure before advising on a live matter.

SECTION 1 — THE INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES ACT, 1947: APPLICABILITY TRIGGERS

The ID Act applies to "industrial disputes" arising in an "industry." Two definitional gateways control whether it applies at all, and several headcount thresholds control which chapters bite.

1.1 Gateway one — is the establishment an "industry"?
Section 2(j) defines "industry" broadly, and its judicial interpretation has been the subject of extensive litigation. The leading authority remains the Supreme Court's seven-judge bench ruling in Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa, which laid down a functional test (organised activity, cooperation between employer and employees, production/distribution of goods or services) rather than a test based on profit motive or the nature of the employer (government department, charitable body, etc.). Sovereign functions and certain statutorily excluded categories remain outside the definition. Because the scope of "industry" has been contested and legislatively revisited over decades, always confirm the current judicial and statutory position before classifying a borderline establishment (e.g., hospitals, educational institutions, clubs, professional firms).

1.2 Gateway two — is the individual a "workman"?
The Act's protections (retrenchment compensation, reference to conciliation/adjudication, reinstatement remedies) attach to persons who fall within the Section 2(s) definition of "workman." Persons employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity are excluded outright. Persons employed in a supervisory capacity are excluded only if their wages exceed a statutory ceiling — commonly cited as ten thousand rupees per month following the 2010 amendment to the Act — so confirm the currently applicable figure, since wage ceilings of this kind are periodically revised and some employees just above or below the line will have their status genuinely contested.

1.3 Headcount thresholds within the Act
Not every chapter of the ID Act applies uniformly regardless of size. Chapter V-B (special provisions on lay-off, retrenchment and closure, requiring prior government permission) applies only to industrial establishments that are factories, mines, or plantations employing 100 or more workmen on average per working day in the preceding twelve months (Section 25K). Several states have used their power to amend central labour legislation to alter this figure for establishments within their territory, so the 100-workman figure cannot be assumed uniformly; the state-specific version in force must be checked. Establishments below the applicable threshold remain subject to the Act's general retrenchment and lay-off provisions (Chapter V-A) but not to the government-permission requirement.

SECTION 2 — THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020: STATUS AND APPLICABILITY

The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 is intended to consolidate and replace the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Trade Unions Act, 1926, and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 into a single instrument. It received Presidential assent on 28 September 2020.

2.1 Commencement is not automatic
The Code, like the other three labour codes (on Wages; Social Security; and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions), takes effect only from a date (or dates, section by section) notified by the central government, and requires state governments to frame their own rules before it is operative in that state. As of any given point in time, the Code may be in force in full, in part, or not at all in a particular state — this status changes and must be independently verified for the relevant jurisdiction and date before relying on it in advice; do not assume it has superseded the ID Act, Trade Unions Act, or Standing Orders Act for a given establishment without checking current notification status.

2.2 Where the Code changes the thresholds practitioners rely on
Subject to the same caveat about commencement, the Code as enacted raises several headcount thresholds that currently govern practice under the older Acts:
- The chapter dealing with lay-off, retrenchment and closure (requiring prior permission) is set to apply to establishments employing 300 or more workers, up from the 100-worker threshold under ID Act Section 25K.
- The requirement to have certified standing orders is set to apply to industrial establishments employing 300 or more workers, up from the 100-workman threshold under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946.
- The Code introduces a statutory concept of a "negotiating union" or "negotiating council": where a single registered trade union has the support of a defined majority of workers — commonly cited as 51 percent — it is entitled to be recognised as the sole negotiating union; where no union crosses that threshold, a proportionally represented negotiating council is constituted. Confirm the applicable percentage and mechanics under the rules actually notified in the relevant state, since implementing detail is set by state rules.
- The Code also revises the definition of "worker," including how supervisory employees are treated for exclusion purposes by reference to a wage ceiling to be notified by the appropriate government rather than a fixed statutory figure; this figure is not static and must be checked against the current notification.

2.3 Practical consequence
Until the Code is confirmed to be in force in the relevant state (and, where relevant, for the specific establishment type), the operative rules remain the ID Act, the Standing Orders Act, and the Trade Unions Act as they currently stand. Treat the Code's provisions as the forward-looking framework to monitor, not as the default current law, unless commencement is confirmed.

SECTION 3 — INDUSTRIAL EMPLOYMENT (STANDING ORDERS) ACT, 1946

3.1 When Standing Orders apply
The IESO Act, 1946 requires employers in an "industrial establishment" to define, in formal Standing Orders, the conditions of employment relating to matters such as classification of workmen, shift working, attendance and late-coming, leave and holidays, termination of employment, and disciplinary action and misconduct — matters that would otherwise be governed by contract or unilateral employer discretion. Section 1(3) sets the baseline applicability threshold at industrial establishments employing 100 or more workmen. Several states have amended this threshold for establishments within their territory (in some cases lowering it), so the number applicable to a given establishment must be confirmed against the state amendment in force, not assumed to be the central figure.

3.2 Certified versus Model Standing Orders
An employer to whom the Act applies must submit draft Standing Orders for certification under Section 3, following a process involving objections from workmen/unions and certification by the Certifying Officer, with an appeal to an appellate authority. Until an employer's own Standing Orders are certified, the Model Standing Orders prescribed under the Act (Section 12A) apply by default and are enforceable exactly as if certified. Employers commonly overlook that the Model Standing Orders are not merely advisory — they bind the employer from the date the Act becomes applicable to the establishment, independent of whether the employer has taken any certification action.

3.3 Interaction with the employment contract
Where Standing Orders (certified or model) apply, their terms are read into every contract of employment between the employer and each workman covered, and they generally prevail over an inconsistent individual contract term to the extent of the inconsistency. This is a frequent point of dispute in termination and disciplinary matters — an employer's internal HR policy or a contractual clause inconsistent with the certified Standing Orders' misconduct/termination procedure is vulnerable to challenge.

SECTION 4 — STATE SHOPS & ESTABLISHMENTS ACTS

4.1 Nature of this layer
Shops and establishments regulation is a state subject. Every state and union territory has its own Shops and Establishments Act (or an equivalent renamed statute), and these differ from each other in definitions, registration procedure, working-hours limits, overtime rules, weekly-off and holiday entitlements, opening/closing hours, employment conditions for women, record-keeping and inspection requirements, and penalty provisions. Examples include the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954, the Karnataka Shops and Commercial Establishments Act, 1961, and Maharashtra's current statute, the Maharashtra Shops and Establishments (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 2017 (which replaced the earlier Bombay Shops and Establishments Act, 1948, as applicable to that state). Because each state's Act is distinct and subject to its own amendments, never assume a rule from one state's Act applies in another; the specific state Act governing the location of the establishment (not the employer's registered office) must be checked.

4.2 What triggers coverage
Coverage typically turns on whether the workplace falls within the state Act's definition of "shop," "commercial establishment," or "establishment" (definitions vary — some states extend coverage to IT/ITES establishments, some carve out specific exemptions for such establishments from certain provisions like working-hour caps, subject to conditions). Registration is generally mandatory once the definition is met, regardless of employee count, though specific obligations (e.g., appointment of a welfare officer, maintenance of particular registers, applicability of certain leave entitlements) may carry their own employee-count thresholds that vary by state. Confirm both the definitional trigger and any count-based sub-thresholds under the specific state Act.

4.3 Relationship to the ID Act/Standing Orders/IR Code layers
A Shops and Establishments Act does not deal with industrial disputes, retrenchment, lay-off, or standing orders — those remain governed by the ID Act/IR Code and the Standing Orders Act/IR Code respectively, where those Acts independently apply to the establishment. An establishment can simultaneously be registered and compliant under its state Shops and Establishments Act and separately be an "industrial establishment" attracting the ID Act and Standing Orders obligations. Treat the two families of statutes as cumulative, not alternative.

SECTION 5 — WORKING THROUGH APPLICABILITY FOR A GIVEN ESTABLISHMENT

For any establishment, the applicability analysis should proceed through each of the following questions, in this order, and the analysis should be re-run whenever headcount, location, or activity changes materially:
1. Does the establishment's activity meet the Section 2(j) "industry" test under the ID Act (as interpreted judicially)? If yes, the ID Act's general provisions (conciliation, adjudication, general retrenchment/lay-off protections) apply regardless of size.
2. Does the establishment meet the applicable headcount threshold (checked against any state amendment) for Chapter V-B of the ID Act (special permission requirements for lay-off/retrenchment/closure)?
3. Does the establishment meet the applicable headcount threshold (checked against any state amendment) for the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, triggering an obligation to certify Standing Orders or operate under Model Standing Orders?
4. Which state's Shops and Establishments Act governs the physical location of the establishment, and does the establishment meet that Act's definitional trigger for coverage (independent of headcount)?
5. Has the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 been brought into force, in whole or in relevant part, for the state and establishment type in question? If so, apply the Code's revised thresholds and mechanisms in place of the ID Act/Standing Orders Act analysis above; if not, or if only partially notified, apply the older Acts for the provisions not yet commenced.

SECTION 6 — COMMON PRACTITIONER CAVEATS

- Headcount thresholds cited in statutory text (100, 300, or otherwise) are frequently altered by state-specific amendments; do not rely on the central figure without checking the state position.
- "Workman"/"worker" status is contested at the margins — managerial, administrative, and supervisory exclusions turn on actual duties performed, not job title, and wage-based exclusions turn on a ceiling that is periodically revised.
- Commencement of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (and the other three Labour Codes) is state- and provision-specific; treat any claim that "the new Codes apply" as requiring independent verification against the current notification position for the relevant state and provision, not as a settled fact.
- Registration under a state Shops and Establishments Act does not exempt an establishment from ID Act, Standing Orders Act, or (once commenced) IR Code obligations, and vice versa; the layers are cumulative.",

{"content":"Slide 1: Lesson Map
- Four sources govern the employment relationship in an Indian industrial/commercial establishment: the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (ID Act); the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (IR Code); the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 (SO Act); and the applicable state Shops & Establishments Act.
- These are not alternatives — a single establishment can be governed by more than one simultaneously, each triggered by different facts (nature of activity, headcount, category of worker, state of incorporation/location).
- This lesson isolates the applicability trigger for each statute, not its substantive obligations.
- Verify current notification/commencement status before advising, particularly for the IR Code 2020 (see Slide 4).

Slide 2: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 — What Triggers Coverage
- Applies where the establishment is an "industry" under Section 2(j) — a broad term covering business, trade, undertaking, manufacture, or calling of employers, and calling, service, employment, handicraft or industrial occupation of workmen. The scope of "industry" has been shaped substantially by judicial interpretation, most notably the Supreme Court's Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa ruling — treat this as a live interpretive question, not a fixed checklist.
- Coverage of an individual is further gated by the definition of "workman" under Section 2(s): persons employed to do manual, unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire/reward are covered; persons employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity are excluded, and supervisory employees drawing wages above a specified monthly threshold are also excluded from "workman" status.
- Certain chapters carry their own headcount triggers layered on top of general applicability — e.g., Chapter V-B (special provisions on lay-off, retrenchment and closure) applies only to industrial establishments employing not less than 100 workmen on average per working day in the preceding 12 months; several states have amended this threshold, so the state-specific figure must be checked, not assumed.
- Retrenchment compensation and notice obligations under Chapter V-A (Section 25F) apply more broadly, keyed to a workman completing one year of continuous service, independent of the 100-workman Chapter V-B threshold.

Slide 3: Consequence of the "Industry" and "Workman" Gates
- An establishment can be a covered "industry" while most of its staff (managers, HR, finance leadership) fall outside "workman" and therefore outside core ID Act protections such as retrenchment compensation and the disputes machinery.
- Practitioners should map roles individually against Section 2(s), not assume department-wide coverage or exclusion.
- Contract labour, apprentices, and probationers each raise separate, fact-specific questions on "workman" status that are commonly litigated — treat as unsettled at the level of a specific fact pattern even where general principles are settled.

Slide 4: Industrial Relations Code, 2020 — Status and Trigger (Caveat First)
- The IR Code, 2020 was passed by Parliament and received Presidential assent in 2020; it is designed to consolidate and replace the ID Act, 1947, the Trade Unions Act, 1926, and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946.
- As of drafting this material, commencement of the IR Code (and the other three Labour Codes) is contingent on separate government notification of effective dates and the framing of central and state Rules; confirm current notification status before relying on the Code as operative law in any given state.
- Once operative, the Code's applicability trigger for standing-orders-type obligations and for the retrenchment/lay-off/closure chapter is raised to industrial establishments employing 300 or more workers, up from the 100-workman threshold under the ID Act/SO Act regime — this is a material shift practitioners should track, not assume is already in force everywhere.
- The Code also introduces explicit statutory recognition of Fixed Term Employment and reorganizes dispute-resolution and strike/lock-out notice provisions; substantive treatment is outside this lesson's scope.

Slide 5: Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 — When It Applies
- Applies to an "industrial establishment" employing 100 or more workmen (Section 1(3)); several states have lowered this threshold by state amendment, so the state-specific figure in force must be checked for the establishment's actual location.
- Where the Act applies, the employer must submit draft Standing Orders to a Certifying Officer for certification (Sections 3–6); until certified Standing Orders are in force, the Model Standing Orders in the Schedule to the Act apply by default.
- Standing Orders must cover prescribed matters: classification of workmen, manner of intimating hours of work, attendance and late-coming, leave and holidays, closure/reopening, termination and notice, suspension and disciplinary action, and grievance procedure.
- Once certified, Standing Orders bind both employer and workmen and cannot be modified except through the procedure prescribed under Section 10 — unilateral employer variation is not effective.

Slide 6: Standing Orders — Practical Applicability Checks
- The 100-workman (or lower state-specific) threshold is counted per industrial establishment, not per employer group-wide; multi-location employers may have some locations covered and others not.
- The Act's trigger is headcount-based and activity-based (industrial establishment as defined), independent of the ID Act's "industry" test — an establishment can be within one and outside the other.
- Where the IR Code, 2020 eventually commences, the operative Standing-Orders-equivalent threshold moves to 300 or more workers; until commencement, the 1946 Act's threshold (as locally amended) governs.

Slide 7: State Shops & Establishments Acts — How They Govern a Workplace
- Shops & Establishments law is a state subject; there is no single central Act — each state/UT has its own statute (e.g., the Maharashtra Shops and Establishments (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 2017; the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954; the Karnataka Shops and Commercial Establishments Act, 1961). The correct statute is determined by the establishment's physical location, not the employer's registered office or the employees' work location if different.
- Coverage extends to shops, commercial establishments, offices, hotels, restaurants, theatres and similar premises — a category distinct from, and not requiring, "industry" status under the ID Act.
- Registration of the establishment with the local authority within a prescribed time from commencement of business is typically the first trigger; the prescribed time period and registering authority vary by state and must be checked against the specific state Act and rules.
- Once registered, the Act typically regulates working hours, weekly/other holidays, overtime, spread-over and rest intervals, leave entitlements, and conditions for employment of women (including night-shift conditions) — several states have issued exemption notifications for specific sectors (e.g., IT/ITES) from parts of these provisions; current exemption status must be verified state-by-state and is subject to change.

Slide 8: Putting the Four Together — Practitioner Checklist
- Step 1: Is the establishment an "industry" under ID Act Section 2(j)? If yes, map which roles are "workmen" under Section 2(s).
- Step 2: Does headcount meet the Standing Orders Act threshold (100 or more, or lower state-amended figure) for the establishment as located? If yes, confirm certified Standing Orders exist or Model Standing Orders apply by default.
- Step 3: Register under, and comply with, the Shops & Establishments Act of the state where the establishment is physically located — this obligation is largely independent of ID Act/SO Act coverage.
- Step 4: Track IR Code, 2020 commencement status separately; do not treat its 300-worker thresholds or consolidated provisions as currently binding until formally notified and in force for the relevant state.
